metadata.title: Day, twilight and night (computed)
metadata.abstract: Night and the three twilights, right now. Computed from the date and time rather than fetched, and redrawn continuously as the Earth turns: the whole picture slides west at 464 metres a second on the equator, gliding at street zoom and barely stirring at world zoom. Where the bands lie north to south is a matter of the date — in June the night side does not reach the Arctic at all — and where they lie east to west is a matter of the time. The bands are set by how far the sun is below the horizon. Civil twilight, down to 6 degrees below, is still bright enough to read outdoors and to make out the horizon at sea. Nautical twilight, 6 to 12 degrees, brings out the brighter stars while the horizon can just be seen — the two together are what a sextant needs, and where the name comes from. Astronomical twilight, 12 to 18 degrees, looks dark but still washes out the faintest stars. Below 18 degrees is full night.

metadata.title: Sun position (computed)
metadata.abstract: The point the sun is directly overhead, right now, moving west at 464 metres a second as the Earth turns. Computed from the date and time rather than fetched, and redrawn continuously — at street zoom it glides across the screen, at world zoom it barely stirs. How far north or south the sun stands is a matter of the date — that is the seasons. How far east or west is a matter of the time: the Earth turns fifteen degrees an hour, so the sun crosses one degree of longitude every four minutes. But the clock is not quite the sun's: because the Earth's orbit is an ellipse and its axis is tilted, the sun reaches its highest point up to a quarter of an hour before or after twelve o'clock, depending on the month. That is taken into account here. Leaving it out shifts the sun up to four degrees of longitude — a quarter of an hour of turning, which measures about 450 km on the equator and less towards the poles.

metadata.title: Sun paths | solstice to solstice
metadata.abstract: The track the overhead sun takes each day, one line per day from the June solstice on the Tropic of Cancer to the December solstice on the Tropic of Capricorn. The return half of the year retraces the same latitudes, so it is not drawn. The lines crowd at the solstices, where the sun turns, and spread at the equinox, where it crosses the equator fastest — the spacing is the seasons.

metadata.title: Graticule
metadata.abstract: Meridians and parallels, sampled so they curve as the projection curves rather than cutting corners.

metadata.title: Equator, tropics and polar circles
metadata.abstract: Computed from the tilt of the Earth on this date. The tilt drifts, so the tropics and polar circles move about ten metres a year — an atlas from 1926 has them half a kilometre out.

metadata.title: Tissot indicatrix
metadata.abstract: Circles of 500 km ground radius. Whatever the projection does to them is what it does to every shape and area on the map: on Mercator they swell towards the poles, on an equal-area map they squash but keep their size.

metadata.title: Hours of daylight
metadata.abstract: Latitudes that get 0, 2, 4 … 24 hours of daylight today. The 0 and 24 hour lines exist only when there is polar night or midnight sun somewhere.

metadata.title: Solar time
metadata.abstract: Where it is solar noon, and every hour of solar time either side. The gap against the clock is why the sun is overhead at half past one in western Spain.

metadata.title: Analemma
metadata.abstract: Where the sun stands at 12:00 UTC on every day of the year: the figure of eight made by the tilt of the axis and the eccentricity of the orbit. Each day is its own segment, and the yellow dot is today.

metadata.title: Moon above the horizon
metadata.abstract: The half of the Earth the moon is above the horizon for. Where this overlaps the night side is where it can actually be seen.

metadata.title: Maanstand
metadata.abstract: Where the moon stands overhead, drawn at the size of the sun marker and shaded to show how much of it is lit. How much is lit is the same for everyone on Earth. Which way the lit side is turned is not: that is measured against somebody's horizon, and directly under the moon there is no such measure, because a point straight overhead has no compass direction. So by itself this marker claims no angle — the terminator simply follows the direction to the sun over the ground, and no horizon is drawn. Click anywhere on the map and it becomes a view instead: the crescent is turned the way it hangs over that place, a horizon appears under it, and a dot marks the place you chose. Click Paramaribo and the horns point up like a boat; click Amsterdam and the same moon stands on its edge. If the moon is below the horizon there, or the sky is bright, it is drawn faintly — nobody there is looking at this. Any click will do, including the info tool's, so no tool has to be switched on for it.

metadata.title: Maanpad
metadata.abstract: The track of the point the moon stands over, for the month that follows the moment shown. The line runs west almost 28 times, once for each turn of the Earth, and swings from about 28 degrees north to 28 degrees south and back once over the month. That swing is the moon's orbit, tilted 5 degrees against the plane the Earth travels in, which is itself tilted 23 degrees against the equator. The two tilts add up or partly cancel depending on where the orbit is pointing, and that turns right around over 18.6 years: in 2024 the moon reached 28.4 degrees, in 2034 it only reaches 18.5. Stone circles at Stonehenge and Callanish are lined up on that same cycle.

metadata.title: Getijdenkracht (evenwichtsgetijde)
metadata.abstract: The shape the sea would take if the water could follow the moon and the sun at once. Two bulges: one under the moon, and one on the far side of the Earth, where the moon's pull is weakest. The sun does the same thing at 46% of the strength — far heavier, but so much further away, and the effect falls off with the cube of the distance. Add the two together and the 28-day cycle of the moon becomes visible: at new moon and at full moon the sun and the moon pull along the same line and their bulges add up, giving the largest tides of the month; a week later, at half moon, they pull at right angles and partly cancel, giving the smallest. The difference between the two is about two to one. The red dots mark the two bulges. They sit near the moon but are dragged towards the sun, by as much as 25 degrees at half moon. There is no matching dot for low water, because the lowest level is not a place but a belt right around the world, a quarter turn away from the bulges — the blue contour lines show it. This is not the tide at any coast. Real water cannot keep up with the pull: it arrives hours late, is amplified or damped by the shape of the sea floor, and turns around points where there is hardly any tide at all — three of them in the North Sea alone. A tide table needs measurements taken at each harbour over years. This map shows the pull, not the water level.
